title: AI for accounting firms: what are CPA firms actually using it for?
description: AI for accounting firms with 40-500 staff: where it pays first, what tools cost, the Section 7216 rules, and who signs off.
topic: AI for accounting and CPA firms
job: AI for accounting and CPA firms
verdict: Most firms now use AI for tax research, document intake or audit review, but few have a written AI policy.[^11][^12]
Accountants keep the signature: tax and audit rule-makers say people must check every AI fact, citation and calculation.[^1][^3]
Client data needs a vendor contract or client consent first; tax code Section 7216 penalties cover return information.[^5][^21]
AI moves staff time from data entry to client work, and demand for accountants is still projected to grow.[^10][^20]
Buy the AI inside your tax and audit software first; build only where your own process is the edge.[^46][^43]

answers.human-role: People keep every judgment that carries a signature: the audit opinion, the return, the advice and the decision to share client data.[^1][^3]
answers.ranked: AI pays first in client document intake and tax research, then in audit first-pass review and month-end close for client accounting work.[^11][^9][^10] The intake and research time savings are vendor claims, so measure your own.[^18]
answers.rules: No law bans AI in a CPA firm, but tax privacy law, Circular 230, the AICPA code and quality standards all govern how you use it.[^1][^5] None of this is legal advice.
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI goes wrong at CPA firms when nobody reads its output closely: fake citations, client data in consumer tools and unchecked client reports are the documented failures.[^39][^1]
answers.buy-or-build: Buy first: the AI inside your tax, audit and practice software covers most work, and you build only where your own process is the edge.[^46][^43]
answers.something-else: Pick something else when your software already has the feature, the step never changes, or the volume is too low to repay the review.[^19][^53]

summary: AI in a certified public accountant (CPA) firm reads client documents, drafts research and workpapers, and flags exceptions; accountants review and sign.[^1][^9] In a 2026 field study, accountants using more AI served more clients and closed books faster.[^10] Review discipline and client-data handling make or break it.[^1][^21]
humanRole: The engagement partner signs the audit opinion and must understand and approve any AI tool used.[^3][^4] The American Institute of CPAs (AICPA) says the auditor stays responsible for the audit and the opinion.[^3]

Preparers and reviewers check every AI-filled field and citation before a return or memo goes out, under Circular 230 due diligence.[^2][^1] The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) warns that blind reliance on AI output may be unreasonable.[^1]

The managing partner owns the firm's AI procedures and tool approvals, under Circular 230 section 10.36 and the quality standard SQMS 1.[^1][^32] The IRS Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) lists training, secure data handling and vendor contracts.[^1]
A tax partner decides client notice and consent before client data reaches an AI vendor.[^5][^23] The AICPA says AI should support, not supplant, professional judgment.[^7]

ranked.name: Client document intake and chasing
ranked.why: In a 2024 survey reported by a vendor, 49% of 240 professionals said gathering documents takes 1-2 days per engagement.[^17] SurePrep's own study claims 1.59 fewer hours per return (vendor claim).[^18]
ranked.payoff: Measure your own: days from first upload to ready-for-prep, and preparer hours per return.

ranked.name: Tax research and memo drafting
ranked.why: Firms using AI tax research rose to 60% from 33% in a year, and 84% say it saves time (vendor survey).[^11] Fake citations are the risk; the IRS says to check citations and read the cases.[^1][^39]
ranked.payoff: Research hours per question and the share of citations that pass a read-through, not the vendor's time claim.

ranked.name: Audit first-pass review: extraction, vouching and tie-out
ranked.why: One 11-person firm cut first-pass document review from about a week to 2-3 hours with a closed AI system, by its own account.[^9] The AICPA's October 2026 practice aid covers AI in the audit and its risks.[^3]
ranked.payoff: Fieldwork hours per engagement and review notes per file.

ranked.name: Client accounting services: bank feeds, reconciliation and close
ranked.why: A 2026 field study of 79 small-business clients tied heavier AI use to about 19% more clients a week and a close 7.5 days faster.[^10] Accountants stepped in when the AI's confidence was low, and time moved to client communication and quality checks.[^10]
ranked.payoff: Days to close per client, clients per accountant and low-confidence items per month.

ranked.name: Workpaper review assist, with AI as the first reviewer
ranked.why: At one firm in a Journal of Accountancy report, AI is the mandatory first reviewer before partner review.[^9] Effort is higher: it needs a firm-approved tool, and Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) staff offer no safe harbor for AI.[^37]
ranked.payoff: Review notes per engagement and partner review hours.

ranked.name: Client emails, engagement letters and practice admin
ranked.why: Karbon survey users report saving 60 minutes a day each (self-reported vendor survey, 593 respondents).[^12] Karbon and TaxDome already build AI into practice management (vendor pages).[^50][^51]
ranked.payoff: Response time to client emails and admin hours per week.

ranked.name: Advisory and planning drafts
ranked.why: Advisory is the top AI tax research use, at 44%, and 69% expect value-based, hybrid or fixed fees (vendor survey).[^11] The partner's judgment carries the advice, so the payoff is harder to measure.[^7]
ranked.payoff: Advisory hours sold per partner and turnaround on planning memos.

ownData.title: What are the largest US CPA firms hiring for?
ownData.intro: The largest US CPA firms still hire mostly tax and audit staff; only about 1 in 80 job posts has AI in the title.[^54] We counted US posts from the last 60 days at 35 large CPA firms, pulled 26 Nov 2026; 24 had posts listed.[^54] Read it as a signal of where the work is heading, not a picture of firms with 40 to 500 staff.

Audit or assurance posts that mention AI
ownData.note: Zavient count from one job-post index, US posts in the 60 days to 26 Nov 2026; 11 of the 35 firms had no posts listed.[^54] A post listed in several cities counts once per city, so shares are of rows, and keyword matching is rough. October and November fall before busy season, when tax hiring may rise.

rules.name: Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10) and OPR's AI guidelines
rules.status: In force; OPR guidelines dated 24 Jun 2026
rules.what: Due diligence, competence and firm-procedure duties apply to AI-assisted work.[^2][^1] OPR's 2026 guidelines say to verify facts, citations and calculations, and to use only enterprise-approved AI.[^1] Billing for time not actually spent may breach section 10.27.[^1]

rules.name: Tax code Sections 7216 and 6713
rules.what: Knowing or reckless disclosure of return information is a misdemeanor; the civil penalty is $250 a disclosure, up to $10,000 a year.[^21][^22] Whether a general AI vendor needs taxpayer consent is unsettled, and the IRS has not said.[^23][^26] Check with your own tax counsel.[^28]

rules.name: Treasury Reg. 301.7216-2 and Rev. Proc. 2013-14 (consent)
rules.what: Disclosures inside the firm in the US need no consent, but sending return data offshore does.[^23][^25] Consent for 1040 returns must name the recipient, the purpose and the information.[^24] For business returns, consent can sit in the engagement letter.[^25]

rules.name: Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314) and your WISP
rules.what: Tax and accounting firms count as financial institutions under this rule, whatever their size.[^29][^31] You need a written information security plan (WISP), multi-factor authentication and service-provider oversight.[^29] List each AI vendor in the plan as a service provider.[^30]

rules.name: AICPA Code of Professional Conduct, ET 1.150.040 and 1.700.040
rules.status: In force for members; updated through Sep 2026
rules.what: Inform clients, preferably in writing, before sharing confidential data with a third-party provider.[^5] Before disclosing, sign a confidentiality contract with the provider or get the client's specific consent.[^5] Whether an AI tool counts as exempt software hosting is unsettled, so notice plus a contract is the safe course.[^5][^6]

rules.name: AICPA quality management standard, SQMS 1
rules.status: In force; systems in place by 15 Dec 2025
rules.what: Software, AI included, counts as a technological resource the firm must govern.[^32] Peer review now looks at quality management.[^33]

rules.name: PCAOB QC 1000 and the technology-assisted analysis amendments
rules.status: QC 1000 effective 15 Dec 2026; amendments for fiscal years from 15 Dec 2025
rules.what: These apply only to firms registered with the PCAOB that audit public companies.[^34][^35] If you audit only private companies, SQMS 1 applies instead.[^32] The amendments cover analysis of electronic data, and PCAOB staff say there is no safe harbor for AI.[^36][^37]

rules.name: AICPA practice aid, AI Considerations for Financial Statement Auditors
rules.what: The practice aid covers AI use in financial statement audits.[^3][^4] The engagement partner should understand the tools and confirm they are firm-approved.[^3]

rules.name: State AI laws and state boards of accountancy
rules.what: No comprehensive federal AI law exists, and most state AI laws target AI developers, not CPA firms.[^38] OPR names California, Colorado, Illinois and Utah as states with AI governance laws.[^1] We found no AI rule from a state board of accountancy, so check with yours.

watchOuts: Fake citations reach filings: a 2026 Tax Court filing cited three AI-invented cases, and a Minnesota court referred a county's fake citations for discipline.[^39][^40] Read every cited case before anything is filed, as the IRS directs.[^1]

Client data pasted into a consumer AI tool risks unauthorized disclosure under Sections 7216 and 6713.[^1][^21] Use an enterprise tool under contract with no training on your data, and list it in your WISP.[^29][^5]

Vendors are asking firms to sell data for AI training, and redaction does not make client information nonconfidential.[^6] Get specific written client consent and run a separate Section 7216 check.[^6][^23]

A Big Four member firm refunded part of an A$440,000 Australian government report with AI errors, and was later barred over another.[^41][^42] Have a named reviewer read every AI-drafted deliverable before it goes out.[^1]

Few firms write it down: only 21% have an AI policy or strategy, and 18% track AI returns (vendor surveys).[^12][^13] Write a one-page policy, train staff, and record two measures for a month before any pilot starts.[^1]

Billing for time AI saved may breach Circular 230 section 10.27, though an IRS advisory council asked OPR to revise that guidance.[^1][^26] Move AI-heavy work to fixed or value fees, as 69% of surveyed accountants expect.[^11]

faq.a: No sign of it yet: the Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 5% job growth for accountants and auditors from 2025 to 2035.[^20] About 115,300 openings are expected each year, and a 2026 field study found AI moved time from data entry to client work.[^20][^10] The largest firms we checked still post mostly tax and audit roles.[^54]

faq.q: Can I put client tax data into ChatGPT?
faq.a: Not into a consumer tool: the IRS says to use only secure, enterprise-approved AI, and Section 7216 penalties apply to unauthorized disclosure.[^1][^21] The AICPA code also requires a vendor confidentiality contract or the client's specific consent.[^5]

faq.q: Do I need taxpayer consent before return data goes to an AI vendor?
faq.a: Not settled: the IRS has not said whether a general AI vendor is an auxiliary service provider that needs no consent.[^23][^26] An IRS advisory council asked for guidance on Section 7216 in November 2026.[^27][^28] Check with your own tax counsel before return data reaches the vendor.

faq.q: Do I have to tell clients I use AI?
faq.a: Yes, usually, if the tool receives confidential client information: the AICPA code says to inform clients first, preferably in writing.[^5] Pure software hosting is exempt and whether AI counts is unsettled, so the AICPA-sponsored insurer suggests disclosing anyway.[^5][^8]

faq.q: Which AI tools do accounting firms actually use?
faq.a: Mostly AI tax research, document scan-and-fill, audit extraction tools and AI built into practice management software.[^11][^9][^12] The tools table above lists prices read on 26 Nov 2026.

faq.q: Can we bill clients for the time AI saved?
faq.a: No, not as if staff did the work by hand: OPR says billing for time not spent may violate Circular 230 section 10.27.[^1] Most surveyed accountants expect value-based, hybrid or fixed fees instead (vendor survey).[^11]

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy for general ledger, practice management and tax prep, and switch on the AI already inside those tools.[^46][^47] Most enterprises now buy: 76% of AI use cases in 2025, up from 53%.[^43] Bought tools reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds in an MIT study.[^44][^45]
buyVsBuild.build: Build only a thin layer that reflects how your firm works, such as your review checklist or research memo template.[^47] CPA.com warns that builds bring shadow IT, cross-client data leakage and key-person risk.[^47]

pickElse: Your tax or audit software already has it: turn on the AI in SurePrep, Caseware or your practice management tool first.[^19][^53]
The step never changes: use rules-based automation in Karbon or TaxDome, or a data tool such as Alteryx or Power BI.[^50][^51] Power BI appeared in 62 of the large-firm posts we counted.[^54]
Seasonal volume is the problem: outsourcing can fit, but offshore work needs Section 7216 consent and an AICPA client notice.[^23][^24][^5]
The task takes an hour a month: skip AI for now, because policy, training and review would cost more than it saves.[^1][^12]

offer.heading: Which job should your firm hand to AI first?
offer.body: The first job is usually high-volume and easy to check, such as document intake, tax research or month-end close for client accounting work. In a free 30-minute call we map that job, who reviews the output and what to measure. You leave with the client-consent and WISP checks to run before any pilot.

reviews.notes: COO: the bottom line answers what firms use AI for, and the human-role block names who signs (engagement partner, preparer, reviewer, managing partner, tax partner). Every ranked job ends in a number to measure. Problem: IRS and AICPA appeared in the bottom line before being spelled out, and FTC never was. Fixed: bottom line 2 now says 'tax and audit rule-makers'; IRS is spelled out in the human-role block (AICPA, OPR and PCAOB already were) and FTC in the rules table. All 18 question headings open with a direct answer; FAQ questions come from the keyword pull (will cpa be replaced by ai, 260 a month), r/taxpros and r/Accounting threads, a CPA insurer FAQ and the IRS guidance.

Head of operations: wants to know what changes in the workflow and where people step in. The document-to-return table shows each hand-off and that nothing is filed until the reviewer signs. Problem: the client accounting item said what improved but not when an accountant steps in, and the policy watch-out gave no baseline step. Fixed: the item now says accountants take the low-confidence items, with low-confidence items per month added to its measures; the watch-out now says to record two measures for a month before a pilot starts.

GM: wants cost and effort before saying yes to a pilot. The tools table gives list prices read 26 Nov 2026 from each vendor's own page, and says 'Not published' where SurePrep and Caseware show none; no Zavient price, per site rules. Buy-or-build says switch on what you already pay for first. Problem: the ranking says payoff then effort, but no item said which one costs more effort. Fixed: the workpaper review item now says its effort is higher and why (a firm-approved tool, no safe harbor).

Tax and audit practice leads: check the rules are stated exactly. Section 7216 consent for a general AI vendor is called unsettled, with the regulation, the IRS Advisory Council request and 'check with your own tax counsel'; the $250 and $10,000 Section 6713 figures were confirmed on the statute text. PCAOB QC 1000 is limited to registered firms, with SQMS 1 named for private-company audits. Problem: FAQ 2 implied Section 7216 penalties attach to any AI use. Fixed: it now says they apply to unauthorized disclosure. Also tightened the Blue J cell, which named CPA.com twice.

Steve: the title is his question and the five bottom-line bullets answer it in about ten seconds, with the signature, client-data and buy-first points up front. The hiring table is clearly labelled as the largest firms, not firms his size, so he is not misled. No Zavient price, per Russell's 26 Nov decision; not flagged. Problem: the summary said 'firms using more AI', but the field study measured accountants. Fixed: it now says accountants using more AI served more clients and closed books faster.

sources.what: Quality control standard for PCAOB-registered firms; effective 15 Dec 2026.

sources.name: SEC order approving PCAOB amendments, Release 34-106791 (Nov 2026)
sources.what: Approves the amendments adopted 9 Sep 2026, including the QC 1000 effective date.

sources.name: PCAOB, amendments on technology-assisted analysis (AS 1105, AS 2301)
sources.what: Effective for audits of fiscal years beginning on or after 15 Dec 2025.

sources.name: PCAOB, Staff Spotlight on generative AI (Jul 2024)
sources.what: Firms mostly use generative AI for admin and research; no safe harbor for AI use.

sources.name: AICPA advocacy, AI Policy After the Elections: The Landscape Heading into 2027
sources.what: No comprehensive federal AI law; state laws mostly aim at AI developers.

sources.name: Journal of Accountancy, A recipe for sanctions: AI-hallucinated citations in tax (1 Sep 2026)
sources.what: A 2026 US Tax Court filing cited three AI-invented cases; the court warned but did not sanction.

sources.name: Minnesota Tax Court, order on sanctions (29 May 2025)
sources.what: Five fake citations in a county's brief; Rule 11 violation; referral to the professional responsibility board.

sources.name: Associated Press, Australian government report partly refunded over AI errors (7 Oct 2025)
sources.what: A Big Four member firm partly refunded an A$440,000 government report with AI errors. Incident only.

sources.name: Sydney Morning Herald, Western Australia three-month ban over AI-flawed report (25 Nov 2026)
sources.what: The same firm barred from Western Australian government work for three months over another AI-flawed report. Incident only.

sources.name: Menlo Ventures, 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise
sources.what: 76% of AI use cases bought in 2025, up from 53% in 2024.

sources.name: MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide (Jul 2025)
sources.what: Bought or partnered tools reached deployment about 67% of the time, internal builds about 33%; 52 interviews.

sources.name: Fortune, coverage of the MIT report (18 Aug 2025)
sources.what: Reports the buy-versus-build deployment gap from the MIT study.

sources.name: CPA.com, AI build vs. buy decision framework (9 Jun 2026)
sources.what: Buy commodity systems such as general ledger, practice management and tax prep; build around configurable platforms.

sources.name: CPA.com, Build vs. Buy: The decision framework for AI in accounting firms (PDF)
sources.what: Build a one-off utility or a core-competency layer; builds risk shadow IT, cross-client data leakage, pricing whiplash and key-person dependence.
